I'm Arnav Hemanth, a final-year Computer Science (Data Science) student at Dayananda Sagar Academy of Technology and Management in Bengaluru, India. Solo entry.

Most of what I've built is aviation predictive maintenance. My main project is EngineWatch (enginewatch.tech), an interpretable engine health monitoring and remaining-useful-life system trained on NASA's C-MAPSS turbofan data. It's deployed and running, not a notebook. The thing I care about there is that every prediction traces back to specific sensors — no deep learning, no post-hoc explanation layer sitting on top of a black box.

I registered because taxi-out is a problem I want to be better at. Engine degradation is slow and physical. Taxi-out is operational — queues, runway configuration, how an airport actually behaves at 07:00 on a Monday. Same tooling, completely different reasoning, and I'd rather learn that against a public leaderboard than on my own.

I'm also curious whether a model you can actually explain stays competitive here. That's the position I've been working from for about a year and I've never tested it somewhere the score is public. If it holds up, I want to write it up for JOAS. If it doesn't, that's worth writing up too.

I registered because taxi-out time is the kind of problem I actually enjoy. It is bounded, it is measurable, and there is nowhere to hide ; the RMSE either comes down or it does not. No steering committee is going to rescue a bad model.

I am not an air traffic management specialist, which I am choosing to treat as an advantage rather than a confession. I come at it as a data person looking at a genuinely messy operational signal. Ground movement, weather, stand allocation, the queue at the holding point, and all of it out in the open where anyone can check the working.

The open science side matters to me as well. Public repo, published method, results other people can pull apart. Far too much of what I do sits behind an NDA. This does not, and that is refreshing.

And honestly, I want to know whether the instincts still hold up against a leaderboard.

I maintain an open, DOI-versioned corpus of aviation occurrence records harmonised from 128 sources, published with full provenance and a deterministic, documented deduplication pipeline. My interest here is the ground-operations side: reconstructing airport state at off-block from movement data is a data-engineering problem before it is a modelling one, and the open-code condition matches how I already work.

Outside work I’m a licensed amateur radio operator (2D0PEY), and most of my projects sit where RF, hardware and data meet. I receive ADS-B at home and built NearestPlane, an ESP32-driven display showing the closest aircraft overhead in real time. I also run a couple of small public data tools of my own, so I’m used to shipping something at the end rather than leaving it in a notebook.

Taxi-out time appealed to me because it’s a genuinely operational problem rather than a synthetic one. The interesting part isn’t the model, it’s the framing: taxi-out is largely a question of how congested the airfield is at the moment a flight goes off-block, so the work sits in representing queue state, traffic in the surrounding window, runway configuration and stand geometry. That’s a much more interesting problem than it first looks.

I registered because the combination of open data, a clearly defined target and a public leaderboard is the best possible way to test whether my intuitions about the problem actually hold up. I’m also committed to the open solutions side. Whatever I produce will go up as a documented public repository, whether or not it finishes anywhere near the top.

We are a multidisciplinary aviation and data science team from Viaratech, combining expertise in aerospace engineering, software and data engineering, machine learning, and aviation operations.

Our team brings together experience from both the aviation industry and large-scale data and technology environments. This gives us an opportunity to approach the challenge not only as a machine-learning prediction problem, but also from the perspective of the physical and operational factors that influence aircraft ground movements.

We decided to participate in the PRC Data Challenge because taxi-out time is a particularly interesting example of a highly variable aviation process where operational conditions, airport configuration, traffic intensity, aircraft characteristics and network effects interact. Developing a model that performs well across 11 major European airports therefore represents both an interesting data-science problem and a practical aviation challenge.

Our objective is to explore a transparent and reproducible modelling approach that combines aviation-domain understanding with data-driven feature engineering and machine-learning methods. We are particularly interested in understanding which operational variables explain taxi-out variability and how well those relationships generalise across different airports and operating conditions.

The challenge also strongly aligns with our interest in open aviation research. Beyond achieving a competitive prediction accuracy, we hope to produce an interpretable and reproducible methodology that contributes useful insights to the wider aviation community.

team_description:
Who I am

Saurabh Nandedkar, an engineer based in Mumbai, India, working in applied ML and infrastructure. Outside work I run an AIS receiver station tracking vessel traffic, and I'm setting up an ADS-B station next — partly to feed back into the networks I take data from.

Why I registered

Two reasons.

The first is that I already spend my spare time on the receiving end of this kind of data. Running an AIS station teaches you quickly how much of the interesting signal is in what the raw messages don't say — gaps, timing, and the state of the world you have to infer around them. Taxi-out is the same shape of problem. The movement records tell you when things happened, not what was happening on the surface; the work is reconstructing runway queues, sequencing and configuration from timestamps alone. That's the part I want to do.

The second is the open-science framing. Open data, public code, and a paper at the end is the right shape for a competition. I'd rather spend a month on something that leaves a public artifact behind.

How I'm approaching it

Solo, in Python. Gradient boosting over engineered features rather than anything exotic — I expect the work to live in feature construction and validation design, not model architecture. Planning month-disjoint splits given that the ranking months sit at both extremes of the year, and bringing in open weather data for the winter cases. Code goes on GitHub regardless of where I place.

team_description:
Who I am. A one-person team. I hold a PhD in geoinformatics from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, where I teach photogrammetry, laser scanning and geospatial data processing. My research has focused on managing and processing very large geospatial datasets — point-cloud data management on Apache Spark, LiDAR classification with machine learning, and spatial indexing for distributed workloads. In industry I work as a geospatial software engineer on production spatial platforms (PostGIS, raster and vector pipelines, cloud deployment). Data science, spatial processing and aviation are the three things I enjoy most, and this challenge happens to sit exactly where they meet.

Why I registered. Taxi-out time is usually modelled as a temporal problem, with the stand–runway pair treated as a categorical key. I think a good part of it is geometric: the actual taxi route from stand to runway threshold, its length, the number of turns and intersections, and the runway crossings along the way. My plan is to build a taxiway graph for all ten airports from open OpenStreetMap aeroway data, derive route-based priors from it, and measure how much they add to a solid gradient-boosting baseline with congestion and runway-configuration features. The question I want to answer, and publish either way, is whether a small, open, geodetically grounded spatial layer is worth as much as the usual temporal feature engineering.

Approach. Open data only, a reproducible pipeline, a public GitHub repository, and a short write-up for the Journal of Open Aviation Science.

We are a multidisciplinary team of four students bringing together three Computer Science students and one Avionics student, with a shared interest in artificial intelligence, data science, aviation and building technology that can solve real-world problems.

Our Computer Science members contribute skills in programming, machine learning, data analysis and model development, while our Avionics member brings an aviation and aircraft-systems perspective that helps us understand the physical and operational context behind the data. As a team, we also have an entrepreneurial mindset through our experience in building technology projects and developing a startup, which has taught us to approach technical problems not only from the perspective of “Can we build it?” but also “Can it work in the real world, and can it create meaningful value?”

This combination is particularly relevant to the PRC Data Challenge. Taxi-out time is not simply a mathematical prediction problem; it is influenced by aircraft, airport operations, traffic and other interconnected operational factors. The challenge therefore gives us an opportunity to combine our different areas of expertise rather than treating data science and aviation as separate disciplines.

We see ourselves as students who are still learning, but who are eager to work on problems where advanced technology, engineering and real-world operational data meet.

We decided to participate in the PRC Data Challenge 2026 because it gives us the opportunity to apply artificial intelligence and data science to a genuine aviation problem rather than working only with classroom or synthetic examples.

This year's challenge focuses on predicting aircraft taxi-out time using real operational data from major European airports. The problem is particularly interesting to us because taxi-out time is affected by multiple interacting factors, making it a meaningful machine-learning problem with a direct connection to aviation operations. EUROCONTROL notes that better prediction of taxi-out time can help identify periods of constrained airport operations and support the assessment of excess fuel burn and CO₂ emissions associated with those conditions.

For our team, the challenge is also an opportunity to bring together our different backgrounds. Our Computer Science members can work on data processing, feature engineering, machine-learning models and evaluation, while our Avionics member can contribute aviation-domain understanding. Our entrepreneurial experience motivates us to look beyond simply producing a prediction and to think about how data-driven insights could eventually support more efficient aviation operations.

We are participating to challenge ourselves against an international community, learn from a real-world aviation dataset, strengthen our ability to build reproducible AI solutions, and explore how our combined technical backgrounds can be applied to problems with practical significance.

Ultimately, we see the PRC Data Challenge as a bridge between what we learn as students and the kind of data-driven engineering problems we hope to solve professionally.
